analysis.one_liner: Removes FDA approval for OxyContin, banning the painkiller from the U.S. market.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban OxyContin never got a hearing or a vote and drew zero cosponsors before the 2005-2006 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have voided the FDA approval of OxyContin, the brand name for controlled-release oxycodone, 45 days after enactment — effectively pulling the drug off the U.S. market entirely [S2][S3]. The bill's findings cite rising abuse, overdoses up 450 percent, stolen tablets, and ads that downplayed fatal risks, and conclude the drug's harms outweigh its benefits [S3]. It was referred to a House committee and its health subcommittee and never went anywhere [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be communities dealing with OxyContin abuse — the bill cites middle- and high-school use as high as 9 percent, overdose increases of 450 percent, and 1.5 million stolen tablets between 2001 and 2003 [S3]. Local law enforcement, which the bill says was overwhelmed by drug-related crime in economically depressed areas, would also gain [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Deems the FDA approval for OxyContin withdrawn 45 days after enactment, legally removing the drug from the commercial market.
Targets a drug whose manufacturer had been cited twice for advertising that downplayed potentially fatal risks of abuse, and whose time-release design abusers easily defeat to get a heroin-like high.
Relieves communities where, per the bill's findings, overdose deaths had surged 450 percent and local law enforcement had been overwhelmed by drug-related crime.

analysis.who_pays: Purdue Pharma would lose its flagship product, a blockbuster painkiller worth billions in annual sales. Patients with severe chronic pain who relied on OxyContin would have to switch to other medications, and pharmacies and wholesalers would lose sales. Taxpayers and insurers would absorb the transition costs of moving patients to alternatives.

drawbacks.text: A blanket ban would cut off an FDA-approved medication that legitimate patients with severe pain used, relying on the sponsor's assertion that alternative pain medicines are widely available — an assertion the bill does not substantiate.

The bill's own findings note that OxyContin gives abusers a heroin-like effect; removing it from pharmacies could push some users toward illicit opioids rather than ending their addiction, something a supply-side ban alone cannot fix.
The bill overrides the normal FDA process — under which the agency weighs a drug's risks against its benefits — with a single legislative decree covering one branded product.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and growing problem — the findings on overdoses, thefts, and misleading marketing were documented [S3] — but it is a blunt instrument. It bans one branded product by name rather than tightening oversight of controlled-release opioids generally, and it rests on the unproven claim that substitutes are readily available for every patient. An honest supporter would concede that legitimate pain patients would bear real costs, and that supply bans alone do not end addiction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to a House committee and then its health subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced the Act to Ban OxyContin in the House on May 5, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
On May 13, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed with no further action recorded.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died in subcommittee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Purdue Pharma is better off: OxyContin stayed on the market and its multi-billion-dollar revenue stream was never touched. Patients who depended on the drug also kept access, while the communities the sponsor sought to protect got no relief from the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Purdue Pharma kept OxyContin on the market

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to withdraw OxyContin's FDA approval and referred it to committee; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 13, 2005 and took no further recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Purdue Pharma
against.what_they_did: Marketed and defended its flagship painkiller; the bill would have stripped its FDA approval and removed the product from the market.

sides.party_line_note: One House Democrat sponsored the bill and no other member of either party signed on, so no party-level support or opposition was ever shown — no votes were taken.

industries.note: The bill would have voided the FDA approval of OxyContin, Purdue's flagship product, wiping out its largest revenue source 45 days after enactment. The company's interest in keeping the drug widely prescribed ran against the communities suffering abuse, overdose, and theft the bill documented.
Dispensers and distributors would lose OxyContin sales and have to absorb inventory changes. Their interest here was commercial, not central to the public-health fight.

industries.industry: Pain management prescribers and their patients
industries.note: Doctors treating severe chronic pain would lose an FDA-approved long-acting opioid and would have to switch patients to alternatives. The bill asserts those alternatives are widely available but offers no evidence.
